lede.text: Australia’s housing argument is fundamentally about whether affordability should be pursued through large scale supply and intervention, or through settings that protect investors, landlords and existing owners. Labor points to a $43 billion agenda and faster building, while critics stress that planned support reaches only 55,000 households over 25 years against much larger unmet need. In Victoria, the Housing Statement Reform Bill 2024 makes the immediate contest concrete, combining rental security, bidding rules, minimum standards and planning changes that Labor supports, Liberals resist, and Greens say should include rent caps. Across the years covered, the emphasis has moved from long term underbuilding and tenancy disputes toward an interventionist politics of delivery, judged by targets, approvals and completed homes rather than announcements alone.

sections.question: What policy changes, government announcements and implementation evidence concern housing across the public record since July 2024?
sections.answer:
The Victorian Parliament debated the **Consumer and Planning Legislation Amendment (Housing Statement Reform) Bill 2024**, an omnibus bill covering rental, consumer and planning law. Government speakers (Labor) framed it as delivering on the 2023 housing statement and the October 2024 "more homes, more opportunity" package, claiming it would repeal "no reason to vacate" clauses at the end of fixed terms, ban all rental bidding, extend notice periods for rent increases and notices to vacate from 60 to 90 days, standardise rental application forms, protect applicants' data, require minimum standards before advertising, mandate smoke alarm checks, and introduce continuing professional development for property professionals. Labor's Enver Erdogan said the government had delivered "more than 130 reforms" and that Melbourne was "the undisputed build-to-rent capital of Australia", citing 73 per cent of build-to-rent apartments nationally. Labor's Chris Couzens praised provisions allowing the minister to continue abandoned planning amendments and giving authorities power to reject incomplete permit applications.

Opposition speakers (Liberal/National) criticised the bill. David Davis (Liberal) moved a reasoned amendment to withdraw and redraft it, arguing it would drive rental providers out of the market; he claimed Victoria's public housing stock fell by 475 homes despite nearly $4 billion spent, and that New South Wales added 10,454 social homes in the same period. Bev McArthur (Liberal) opposed repealing no-reason notices to vacate, saying 70 per cent of rental providers own one property and nearly 20 per cent are teachers or nurses. The Greens supported the bill but said it omitted rent caps; Sam Hibbins (Greens) called it "a step in the right direction". The record also includes a Victorian question from 2026 where the Greens pressed the government on its 2024 commitment to let councils regulate short-stay accommodation, noting it was "now mid-2026" and asking whether it would follow through.

On the Commonwealth record, the material is thinner. In a December 2025 Senate estimates (Community Affairs Legislation Committee), a senator asked the Department of Social Services about machinery-of-government changes transferring housing functions to Treasury and disability functions to the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, seeking mechanisms to ensure "no gaps in reporting" from July 2024. In February 2026 estimates (Economics Legislation Committee, Treasury portfolio), officials confirmed responsibility for the National Urban Policy and national cities policy moved to the Housing Group within Treasury. A separate estimates exchange noted planning ministers had met three times since May 2022 — on 27 July 2023, 22 February 2024 and 8 August 2025. The record also includes a government statement that the ABS independently decided not to release 2023-24 Survey of Income and Housing statistics due to data quality issues, and a New South Wales second reading speech by Minister Rose Jackson (Labor) for the Housing Amendment Bill 2025, giving the Minister for Housing powers equivalent to the Land and Housing Corporation to support the "Building Homes for NSW" program.

sections.question: What do bills, government releases, contracts, grants and disclosure records reveal about housing, and what remains unproven since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Bills, government releases, and related records since July 2024 show housing activity across planning, approvals, construction, and tenancy reform, but they do not prove that announced projects have been delivered or that funding has flowed. Under the Infill Affordable Housing pathway, there are currently 29 projects under assessment which, if approved, would deliver approximately 8,000 homes, including 2,400 affordable homes. Nine affordable housing projects have been determined since 1 July 2024, which once constructed will deliver 2,010 homes, including 536 affordable homes — the phrase "once constructed" indicates these are not yet built. Since being established in December 2024, the Housing Delivery Authority has evaluated more than 1,100 expressions of interest from industry, identifying proposals that "can be assessed and constructed quickly," but evaluation is not approval or construction.

The NSW Government has announced targets and processes rather than completed outcomes. In 2024, the Minns Government set new housing targets for regional NSW of 55,000 homes by 2029. Historic reforms passed in 2024 are further transforming the rental market by banning no-grounds evictions, limiting rent increases to once per year, making it easier to have pets, and prohibiting fees for background checks. The introduction of the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill 2024 will complement initiatives including a Rental Taskforce within NSW Fair Trading, the free online Rent Check website, and development of a Portable Rental Bond Scheme. A competition for a Pattern Book opened on 2 July 2024, with the final Pattern Book to be launched in 2025. Since 1 July 2024, Building Commission NSW has received almost 400 reports of alleged unlicensed or unregistered trade work, and since 1 July 2025 there have been 13 deaths in the construction industry in NSW alone.

The record also contains unproven claims and contested matters. A Senate motion on 19 November 2024 noted that an order for production of documents requiring the Minister representing the Treasurer to provide reports prepared by external consultants on planning reforms for the Housing Accord had not been complied with, and rejected the Treasurer's claim of public interest immunity; the motion passed 45–21. On 11 September 2024, the Senate voted against referring the Housing Investment Probity Bill 2024 to committee, meaning the bill was not referred. A report found dwelling prices and rents rose in 2024 but at a slower rate than in 2023, and that supply forecasts do not directly incorporate the impacts of recent state government policy measures such as the Low and Mid Rise policy or Transport-Oriented Development. Rising financing and construction costs reduced the financial feasibility of new residential construction projects in 2024, limiting approvals, commencements, and completions.

sections.question: What have MPs said about housing affordability and home ownership since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several MPs addressed housing affordability and home ownership. In the New South Wales Parliament, a Greens MP (the record does not name the speaker) said the party would not block the Help to Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill 2025, which allows the Commonwealth shared equity scheme to operate in NSW. The MP argued that demand-side subsidies are "inflationary" and "push up the cost of housing," citing economist John Quiggin's evidence that "the money is eventually capitalised into house prices, so the beneficiaries gain at the expense of everyone else." The MP also said housing is "a human right" and criticised the focus on home ownership as "the end goal."

An Opposition MP in the NSW Parliament supported the same bill but criticised the Minns Labor Government for closing the NSW Shared Equity Home Buyer scheme on 30 June 2024, including for domestic violence victims, and for abolishing the First Home Buyer Choice scheme. The MP noted the Help to Buy price cap is $1.3 million for Sydney and regional centres and $800,000 for the rest of NSW, and claimed the government was already 14,001 homes short of its six-monthly National Housing Accord target as of 31 December 2024.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, a Labor MP said the Albanese government is "implementing a now $43 billion agenda" on housing and has been "the boldest and most ambitious Australian government on housing since the Second World War." Another Labor MP said the government inherited a "housing horror show" from the Coalition, citing building costs rising at 17 per cent. A Coalition MP claimed that under the government's housing policies, "older women are the fastest-growing group of homeless Australians—up to almost 40 per cent in a decade." A Northern Territory MP (party not stated) said the five per cent deposit scheme "has already helped more than 1,800 Territorians move into their first home," with price caps rising to $750,000 for Greater Darwin and $600,000 for the rest of the Territory from 1 July.

In the Victorian Parliament, a Liberal MP said that after "11 years of Labor," the "dream of a home is slipping away for our next generations," and that the Liberal-Nationals team would "cut red tape" and lift support for first home buyers. A Greens MP in the NSW Parliament also spoke on the Community Housing Providers (Adoption of National Law) Amendment Bill 2025, saying the party would not oppose it but would advocate for amendments, including making affordable housing permanent rather than allowing it to return to the regular market after 15 years.

sections.question: What positions have been taken on negative gearing and property tax concessions since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Government speakers—including the Prime Minister, the Treasurer, and Labor senators—have consistently defended the reforms as a way to "level the playing field for first home buyers" while protecting existing investors. The Treasurer stated the government is "reforming negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions" and that, from 1 July 2027, negative gearing for residential property will be limited to new builds, with the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount replaced by "inflation adjusted indexation" and a "30 per cent minimum tax" on realised gains. A Labor senator said the changes are "grandfathered, meaning that Australians who currently own investment properties or negatively gear will not be affected," and that the reform is expected to "support around 75,000 Australians into homeownership over the next decade." The Prime Minister told a listener that if she "still has that property and it's negatively geared, she can keep negatively gearing it," and that future investors can still use negative gearing "just needs to be a new build."

Coalition members opposed the reforms. One coalition senator moved a motion seeking Treasury advice on the impact of "changes to housing taxes or lower tax concessions" on supply and rents. Another coalition speaker claimed the government's planned "wholesale changes" to trusts "will cripple nearly 300,000 small businesses," and that the Prime Minister and Treasurer "attacked negative gearing and have gutted capital gains tax concessions—all while doing nothing about bracket creep." A third coalition speaker said the coalition believes "the tax system should continue to favour the person buying their next investment property over young Australians trying to buy a place to live," a position the government characterised as "being locked out."

A crossbench or minor party speaker argued that "the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing, as currently designed, are worsening intergenerational inequity," and that these concessions "overwhelmingly benefit older and wealthier Australians." The same speaker welcomed the government's ambition but noted that "new houses cannot be built in a vacuum" and welcomed budget money for "critical enabling infrastructure." A separate speaker from the Greens criticised that "tax breaks for landlords and investors—including negative gearing and other concessions—exceeded $12 billion," more than Commonwealth investment in social housing, homelessness services, and rent assistance combined.

sections.question: What has parliament said about social and public housing supply since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Across several parliaments, the record shows a mix of claims about social and public housing supply. In the New South Wales Parliament, Minister for Housing Rose Jackson (Labor) said her government delivered 849 new public homes in 2023-24, which she called "the largest number of homes delivered over the past decade," and that it was on track to match that figure in the following year. She also contrasted this with the previous government, which she said sold over $3.6 billion of public housing, and cited a drop to only 194 homes delivered in 2019-20. In a separate NSW speech, Minister Jackson said the government was on track to deliver 850 new social homes in year one of the Building Homes for NSW program, which aims to build 8,400 social homes by 2031 alongside 21,000 affordable and market homes.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, a government minister claimed the $43 billion Homes for Australia plan was delivering more than 5,000 completed homes with Commonwealth investment and another 25,000 in planning or construction, including over 600 new social and affordable homes in Tasmania via the Housing Australia Future Fund. However, at a 2026 estimates hearing, an opposition senator challenged the scale of delivery, noting around 190,000 households were on the public housing waitlist and arguing the government's plan to support "at most 55,000 households" over 25 years "does not match the scale of demand." The senator also claimed the previous Liberal National government oversaw a net reduction in public housing from 110,805 in 2014 to 95,765 in 2023.

The record also contains specific delivery figures. At a Commonwealth estimates hearing, it was reported that under the Infill Affordable Housing pathway there were 29 projects under assessment that could deliver approximately 8,000 homes, and that nine affordable housing projects determined since 1 July 2024 would deliver 2,010 homes, including 536 affordable homes. In NSW, Minister Jackson reported regional delivery rising from 416 homes in 2023-24 to 466 the following year, with 749 homes on track for 2025-26. The record is otherwise limited on broader parliamentary debate about social housing supply, with much of the material focused on specific programs or state-level announcements.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Energy policy and housing?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate shows energy and housing are deeply intertwined, with speakers trading accusations over policy failures. In the NSW Parliament, Minister for Planning and Public Spaces acknowledged the Government "is not supportive of banning new gas connections, because households should have choice," while noting the state's Energy Savings Scheme and Consumer Energy Strategy support electrification. The Minister also cited that "35 per cent of our energy is already from renewable sources" and that NSW "became the first State to mandate seven‑star thermal performance for all new homes," projecting savings of approximately $1,070 per year on energy bills. In the same NSW Parliament, Greens MP Abigail Boyd moved a motion congratulating the Victorian and ACT Governments and various NSW councils for mandating electrification, and called on the NSW Government to "ban new gas connections for residential and commercial developments and require higher standards of energy efficiency for rentals." She cited the Net Zero Commission's 2024 report finding NSW "is not on track to meet emission reduction targets" and that the built environment sector "is the worst performer, having nearly doubled greenhouse gas emissions between 2005 and 2022."

In the Commonwealth Parliament, a government minister criticised the Coalition's housing stance, saying "The Liberals have said they want Australians to raid their super to buy a home," and quoted Saul Eslake as calling that "the worst public policy idea in 60 years in our country." The minister also attacked former Coalition figures, claiming Malcolm Turnbull "said the answer for young people trying to get into their own home was that parents should shell out to help their kids" and that Joe Hockey advised young people to "'Get a good job that pays good money.'" The minister framed the government as "the most active and engaged governments we've seen in the post-war years" on housing, while an opposition speaker in the NSW Parliament accused the Minns Labor Government of "legislat[ing] ambition without resourcing it," citing the 1.2 million homes commitment and the 82 per cent renewables target as examples of outcomes that "ain't gonna happen." The record is limited on direct parliamentary statements linking energy policy and housing beyond these exchanges, which are largely partisan claims rather than settled findings.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Responses and housing?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on housing has centred on the need for more supply and on the conduct of the major parties. A government minister, responding to questions, said the answer to the housing crisis is to "build more homes more quickly", citing new housing starts up 17 per cent on a year ago and a "$43 billion housing agenda" focused on building. The minister also claimed the coalition had "been consistently housing hypocrites", voting against the Housing Australia Future Fund and blocking action, while stating the government's door was open to work with the coalition. A separate government speaker described the Commonwealth's agenda as "$45 billion" and "the boldest and most ambitious housing agenda that a Commonwealth government has had since the postwar period".

In the New South Wales Parliament, debate covered the Housing Amendment (Ministerial Housing Functions) Bill 2026. The minister in reply said the bill gives the Minister for Housing the same functions as the Land and Housing Corporation, supports Homes NSW and the "Building Homes for NSW" program to build 8,400 new social homes and 21,000 new affordable and market homes, and unlocks a "$4 billion investment". He criticised the former government's Land and Housing Corporation for "cannibalising its own capital and properties to self-fund its operation" and actively selling public housing. The bill was read a third time and passed.

The Greens, in the Commonwealth Parliament, proposed amendments to a housing bill, arguing for yearly analysis of system-level allocation data to ensure affordable housing goes to low and very low income households, citing a 2019 Grattan Institute finding that only half of National Rental Affordability Scheme properties went to the poorest 20 per cent of households. The amendments were negatived. A Greens member also criticised the Liberals for proposing Australians "raid their super to buy a home", calling it, via Saul Eslake, "the worst public policy idea in 60 years". A separate NSW ministerial statement noted that the number and mix of housing to be delivered under a planning proposal would be determined later, following departmental assessment.

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on housing between 1993 and 2009?
eras.answer:
A recurring partisan debate over housing policy, with Labor speakers consistently criticising the Howard government's record and defending the Rudd government's initiatives. A Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) claimed the Howard government had "12 years of neglect in the area of housing," citing "cumulative cuts of almost $4 billion in real terms to the Commonwealth-State Housing Agreement," a "$50 million" cut in 1997-98, and the removal of GST compensation in 2003-04. Another Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) said the Howard government had "a consistent policy of neglect" on housing, with no minister and no coordinated approach. Labor speakers also referenced the Industry Commission's 1993 report on public housing, with one noting its finding that "the provision of public housing is a cost-effective way to meet government housing objectives" (Commonwealth Senate), and another quoting its opening line, "'Housing is a basic human need'" (Commonwealth House of Representatives).

Government and opposition speakers debated specific policy responses. A Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) defended the Rudd government's actions, including appointing a housing minister, the National Rental Affordability Scheme (NRAS), and a "$2.2 billion affordable housing package." Another Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) supported the NRAS bills, describing them as part of the response to "the national housing affordability crisis." A coalition speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) supported the NRAS legislation but criticised a lack of detail, noting concerns about the unspecified income test and market rent definition, and argued the scheme was "unlikely to be able to fill the gap" given a forecast need for "more than 200,000 new dwellings by 2009-10." A Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) also noted that the NRAS built on "increased cooperation between the Commonwealth and the states since November last year," including the Council of Australian Governments Housing Working Group.

The record also captures earlier criticisms of the Howard government's approach. A Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) in 2000 detailed the government's handling of the GST on caravan park residents, quoting the ACCC that long-term residents were "classified as occupying commercial residential premises," and arguing they should receive "equal treatment with all other Australians." Another Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) cited falling public housing stock under the Commonwealth-State Housing Agreement, from "372,134 in 1996 to 345,000 units as at the last available figures in 2003-04." A further Labor speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) noted that "funds for public housing have declined rapidly in real terms," with the federal contribution in 2003-04 being "25 per cent less in real terms than it was in 1995-96." The record also includes a coalition speaker (Commonwealth House of Representatives) attributing the housing shortage partly to "deliberate restrictions on the release of land for new housing by state governments" and to high government taxes and charges.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on housing between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Residential Tenancies Amendment (Review) Bill 2018, Housing Affordability and Residential Tenancies Amendment (Social Housing) Bill 2018.
eras.answer:
The New South Wales Parliament debated two distinct housing bills in 2018. The Residential Tenancies Amendment (Review) Bill 2018 aimed to reform private tenancy law, with the Minister in reply describing it as "a comprehensive package of reforms to ensure that tenants can make a house their home and will increase protections for the most vulnerable tenants." The Minister said it provided "greater protections for victims of domestic violence," introduced "minimum standards for properties," made "it easier for tenants to obtain repairs," restricted "rent increases for periodic leases to once every 12 months," and introduced "easier and more robust dispute resolution processes." However, opposition and crossbench members criticised the bill. One Labor member called it "a tremendous disappointment," arguing that "only Labor has a clear policy" on security of tenure and that "a Labor government will outlaw no-grounds eviction." The same member claimed the bill showed the Government was "in thrall to property interests." A Greens member in the Legislative Council said that if the bill were serious about restoring balance it "would end no grounds evictions," and moved an amendment for a further statutory review of the Act, which was not carried.

The Residential Tenancies Amendment (Social Housing) Bill 2018, introduced by the Minister for Family and Community Services and Social Housing, Pru Goward, was described by her as "integral to the Government's vision of a fairer, safer and more sustainable social housing system." It implemented parts of the "Future Directions for Social Housing in NSW strategy." The bill introduced a "risk-based rental bond scheme" targeting tenants who caused significant damage, required the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal to terminate tenancies where a tenant was "convicted of rental rebate fraud" unless exceptional circumstances existed, and gave the Secretary of the Department of Family and Community Services power to investigate and prosecute "private rental subsidy fraud." Government speakers supported the bill, arguing it targeted only "a small minority of tenants who do not value their property" and that "good tenants are sick of having their public spaces damaged." The Legislation Review Committee, however, referred to Parliament "whether the requirement for some social housing tenants to pay a rental bond unduly trespasses on their right to housing," and noted the bill deferred substantive matters such as the "definition of 'class of tenant'" and "the amount of the rental bond" to ministerial guidelines rather than principal legislation. One Labor member, while not opposing the bill, raised concerns about "fairness and due process," including the retrospective application of bonds and the removal of the tribunal's discretion, while another Labor member argued the State was "simply not housing all our citizens adequately," citing a decline in social housing dwellings and increased homelessness between the 2011 and 2016 censuses.

A later 2019 bill, the Better Regulation Legislation Amendment Bill 2019, made technical amendments to clarify the operation of the 2018 tenancy reforms, including provisions ensuring "a domestic violence victim is not liable in any circumstances for property damage caused by a perpetrator," clarifying "that only domestic violence victims can terminate their tenancy on domestic violence grounds," and allowing regulations to prescribe responsibilities for smoke alarms following a coronial inquest. The record also contains a 2010 motion from the Legislative Council referring housing affordability matters to a committee, including "the impact of the First Home Owners Scheme" and "Commonwealth policies that impact the housing market," but provides no further detail on that inquiry's outcome.

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on housing between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included Public Housing, Affordable Housing and HomeBuilder Program.
eras.answer:
Housing policy and debate evolved across several fronts between 2020 and mid-2024, with the Commonwealth and South Australia both featuring. In South Australia, the Marshall Liberal government produced “Our Housing Future Strategy 2020-2030,” published late in 2019, which set out a 10-year housing future including affordable housing initiatives. The Minister for Human Services reported two such initiatives underway: “the thousand new home ownership opportunities to low and medium-income earners by 2025,” a partnership between builders and developers, and an earlier program of “70 affordable homes, through the 2019-20 budget.” The minister also detailed the condition of public housing, noting the stock averaged some 40 years old, and criticised the former Labor government for using “Housing Trust stock as an ATM,” selling some “7,500 properties for $1.5 billion.” The minister claimed the annual sales rate had been reduced from around 600 to 150, aiming for net zero. However, an opposition member countered that under the previous government’s 1,000 affordable homes program, due to end in 2025, “over the past two years less than 60 have been sold,” calling it “a very slow output, very low yield result.”

On the Commonwealth HomeBuilder program, the record includes a ministerial defence and opposition criticism. The minister cited that “the HomeBuilder program has seen detached housing sales increase by 31 per cent” and loan approvals for new housing up by 20 per cent into the September quarter, the highest level for 10 years, supporting the residential construction industry. In contrast, an opposition question referenced Domain stories calling HomeBuilder “‘the most-complex least-equitable construction jobs program ever devised’” and asked whether it should be renamed “home blunder.” A later passage notes the scheme “has been closed since 14 April 2021,” with the only substantive change being a decision by the previous Coalition government, likely in very late 2020, to extend it for about three months at a lower value threshold. The record also reveals that in 2024, the Queensland Labor Treasurer, Cameron Dick, wrote to federal Labor housing minister Julie Collins asking her to “‘urgently consult with states and territories’” and stating that “‘a 12-month extension at the April 30, 2024 deadline for HomeBuilder was required.’”

The Commonwealth debate also centred on the Housing Australia Future Fund and related legislation. A government speaker described the “Housing Australia Future Fund Bill, the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council Bill and the Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023” as “some of the most significant housing reforms we have seen in the last decade,” with the Future Fund creating a “$10 billion funding stream” for social and affordable housing, including for Indigenous Australians, women and children experiencing domestic and family violence, older women at risk of homelessness, and veterans. Another speaker framed the bills as transforming the National Housing Finance and Investment Corporation into Housing Australia and establishing the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council to provide independent advice. The government publicly consulted on the package from 19 December 2022 to 11 January 2023, receiving 46 written submissions and holding three consultation sessions. One speaker argued that housing affordability “is not a problem that we can solve simply by throwing money at it,” requiring “a transparent, non-political, evidence based process,” while another criticised the Coalition for a “lost decade of minimal intervention and investment in social and affordable housing,” asking where their housing investments were across 2013 to May 2022.

key_moments.title: Matters of Public Interest
key_moments.speaker: Scott Ludlam
key_moments.brief: The speaker argued for a national plan to deliver affordable housing, supporting the Australians for Affordable Housing alliance’s six-point plan, and highlighted a shortfall of 90,000 homes requiring $24 billion, while criticizing the lack of a dedicated housing minister and $50 billion in annual tax concessions that inflate house prices.

key_moments.title: Housing Affordability
key_moments.speaker: Jo Haylen
key_moments.brief: The speaker argued that housing affordability is a critical economic and social justice issue, noting that renters in New South Wales lack protections such as longer fixed-term tenancies and safeguards against unjustified rent increases. They praised the Tenants Union of New South Wales for its 40 years of advocacy and called for policy reforms including reviewing six-month leases, allowing pets and minor alterations, and addressing federal capital gains tax and negative gearing.

key_moments.title: Social Housing
key_moments.speaker: John Sidoti
key_moments.brief: Minister Pru Goward defended the government's social housing record, citing the $22 billion Communities Plus program for 23,000 new and replacement social housing dwellings, the Social and Affordable Housing Fund for 3,400 dwellings, and a 43% increase in homelessness funding. She also criticised Labor for selling over 1,700 social housing properties between 2008 and 2010 and for inconsistencies in the member for Bankstown's press release, noting the Opposition Leader had previously endorsed transferring stock to the community housing sector.

key_moments.title: Homelessness
key_moments.speaker: Ryan Park
key_moments.brief: Homelessness was attributed to a lack of social housing, citing a 37% increase in NSW from 2011 to 2016, with investment in social housing argued to support local jobs and economies. The speech acknowledged the 2025 target to halve rough sleeping, highlighted the case of an 80-year-old pensioner facing eviction, and praised local services led by Narelle Clay, Kathy Colyer, and Mandy Booker.

key_moments.title: Social and Affordable Housing
key_moments.speaker: David Layzell
key_moments.brief: The New South Wales Government announced $183 million in additional funding for social housing, on top of $900 million from the previous COVID-19 stimulus budget, and has increased social housing stock by 10 per cent since taking office. Minister Pavey cited 73 homes under construction in St Marys, 1,600 new air conditioners, 900 hydro panels, and 5,000 solar panels installed, while contrasting New South Wales’ 150,000 social housing homes with Victoria’s 80,000.

key_moments.title: Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023
key_moments.speaker: Don Farrell
key_moments.brief: The government introduced the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023, establishing a $10 billion fund to generate up to $500 million annually for building 30,000 social and affordable homes over five years, alongside the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council Bill 2023 to provide independent housing advice, and the Treasury Laws Amendment (Housing Measures No. 1) Bill 2023 to rename NHFIC as Housing Australia.
key_moments.why: Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023, Federal, 2023

key_moments.title: Help To Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill
key_moments.speaker: Sandy Bolton
key_moments.brief: The speaker supported the bill to refer powers for the Help to Buy scheme, which would assist 40,000 participants nationally (2,000 in Queensland) through up to 40% Commonwealth shared equity, but noted criticisms from economist John Quiggin that subsidies are undesirable, the scheme has a lottery character, and social housing should be prioritised, while arguing the scheme is too small to address the housing crisis.
key_moments.why: Help To Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill, Queensland, 2024
